paragraphs.heading: Roblox Company Research
paragraphs.text: Roblox builds a platform for creating, participating and hosting video game experiences with the global community. For this application, it's looking for work in the field of engineering that makes those experiences responsive and gives creators useful tools. The Summer 2027 internship offers a twelve-week project with mentorship and responsibility through implementation, testing, deployment, and presentation. That makes my production software work and interactive projects a useful combination to emphasize. [1]

Doing some research on my own, I found Andrew Swerdlow's February 2025 article which explains how Roblox supports engineers with tools for deploying services, reviewing code, and understanding software behavior. It describes automated canary analysis, which checks a limited release before a change reaches more users. This is a concept similar to the work I’ve done at Phoebe where I was working on model evaluations. Both involve finding evidence of problems before going through with a change. In the letter, I will connect that approach to my changes on the v3 agent harness at Phoebe and the way I rolled changes out for it obviously without implying that I have built Roblox's release systems already. [2]

I also found an article by Anirudh Sudarshan and Anying Li's from June 2025 which describes making Cube 3D generation faster through profiling and avoiding repeated computation. Their broader point is that waiting for things to load and happen interrupts a creator's ability to experiment. I will use that observation to connect Roblox's priorities to Coach Bob, where movement, visual targets and spoken feedback form one interaction that often needed to happen in real-time or near-real-time. It also supports my interest in measurable performance improvements. These two engineering articles let me explain why Roblox's work interests me through concrete examples, rather than relying on its popularity or love for the platform.

paragraphs.heading: Cover Letter Comparison
paragraphs.text: Claude did well at organizing my letter around the same two areas as my original: measurable performance improvements and real-time spatial computing. It connected my Phoebe experience to Roblox’s engineering articles and kept the token and rendering results tied to their test conditions. However, the long performance paragraph reads like my résumé bullets joined together, and phrases such as “a mentor to argue with” are too casual for this application. It also incorrectly claims that both spatial projects used Python and C++, and exaggerates the evidence by saying my evaluations made the Phoebe changes safe. I would keep the two-area structure and relevant company research while removing unsupported claims and giving Phoebe and Coach Bob more room to explain why the work matters. This experience showed me that AI can be useful for organizing a first draft, identifying connections between my experience and a job posting, and suggesting clearer wording. It can also help me notice repetition or gaps that I miss when reviewing my own writing. I would not use it to recite accomplishments since it seems to still hallucinate, explain technical work it does not understand, or write personal reflections that I don’t actually stand behind. Submitting its output without checking it could leave me defending claims in an interview that are inaccurate or not mine which is not a good look for any job. For job applications, I see AI as an editing partner and tool to get from nothing to first draft but not to a submittable final version. I should remain responsible for the facts, the voice, and the final decisions so the application represents someone I can confidently be in the interview.

paragraphs.heading: Online Portfolio Reflection
paragraphs.text: I changed my portfolio from a personal notebook centered on school projects into a clearer overview of my engineering work. In the earlier version (which was severely outdated) the homepage introduces me as a high school student and gives longer descriptions of TensorForest and my robotics team. The current homepage uses a shorter Waterloo introduction followed by concise experience bullets reflecting what is seen on my resume and cover letters, including Phoebe, Extrian, Hack the North and community leadership. This makes my recent work easier to find.

Visually, I replaced the dotted background and colored navigation highlights with a mostly black-and-white design, larger serif headings, and cleaner style. I also added a Sidequests link, giving personal interests a separate place in the navigation. The projects page changed from two large cards to a longer list with dates, categories, short descriptions, and images beside each entry. Coach Bob now appears first, making my AR work more visible to a recruiter, particularly for Roblox. The homepage also includes an Experiences section with direct links to selected work. Together, these changes give visitors more evidence of what I build while keeping my personality present.
